Dispersion: Start with a fact that surprised economists when plant-level data first arrived. Take the Island's weaving industry: four thousand plants try to enter, with productivity, output for given inputs, spread out like this. The ones that survive are those that can cover their costs. Among the survivors, the plant at the ninetieth percentile produces 1.93 times as much as the plant at the tenth from the same labour, capital and materials. Nearly twice the output, from the same inputs, in the same industry. That number was planted to match the data: Chad Syverson, surveying the evidence, reports that within narrowly defined American manufacturing industries the ninetieth-percentile plant makes on average about 1.92 times as much as the tenth with the same measured inputs, and the gaps are larger still in China and India.

Why do the laggards survive? Part of the answer is competition. When buyers can switch easily between plants, sales flow to the best ones, and the worst cannot cover their costs. On the Island, with easy switching, the survivors' ninety-ten ratio falls to 1.36; when switching is hard, it is 2.76. Distance, loyalty, differentiated products, protection from imports, and owners content with less all let weak plants live. Syverson showed it with ready-mixed concrete, which cannot travel far before it sets: in denser markets, where buyers have more plants within reach, productivity is less dispersed and higher on average. But competition explains only part of the gap. The rest, the next chapters argue, is management.
Measuring: If management matters, it has to be measured, and for a long time economists thought it could not be. Nicholas Bloom and John Van Reenen built a way. They score eighteen basic practices in four groups: operations, whether the process is lean and defects are tracked; monitoring, whether results are measured, reviewed and acted on; targets, whether goals are stretching and understood; and people, whether good performers are rewarded and poor ones moved on. Each practice gets a score from one, no practice, to five, best practice. The scores come from a long telephone interview with a plant manager, with open questions, so the manager does not know what a good answer is, and the interviewer never sees the firm's accounts. The survey has since covered thousands of firms in dozens of countries.

Here is the survey run on the Island's fifteen hundred firms. Each dot is a firm: its management score against its productivity. Better-managed firms are more productive: 0.23 log points per point of score. On the Island that slope was planted, and it is causal by construction. In real survey data the same pattern appears, but a correlation alone cannot say which way it runs: profitable firms may simply afford consultants. By owner, multinationals and firms with dispersed shareholders score highest; family firms run by a family chief executive, and government firms, lowest. Those patterns were planted to echo the survey's real findings: across countries the United States scores highest on average, family firms that hand the top job to the eldest son score low, and firms facing more competition are better managed. Whether the scores cause productivity needs an experiment: chapter four.
PlayIt: Chapter three. Play it: four practices and a budget.

Your turn. You own one of the Island's weaving plants, with eight million dollars of sales a year, and you can afford one change. A: record every defect and act on it, for sixty thousand dollars of consultants' and managers' time; it raises output eight percent when it works. B: count your stock and cut it, for forty thousand, freeing a third of the inventory. C: a faster loom, six hundred thousand dollars, ten percent more output, and almost sure to work. D: pay workers for performance, a hundred and fifty thousand to design and run, six percent more output, but it works only sixty percent of the time. Which pays the most for each dollar it costs, over three years?

Here is what each change is worth over three years, per dollar it costs. A, recording and acting on defects, returns 4.6 dollars of net value for every dollar: about 278 thousand dollars. B, cutting inventory, 3.0 per dollar. C, the loom, the most visible investment, loses money over three years: it pays back eventually, but slowly. D, pay for performance, returns 0.21 per dollar on average, with a wide spread: incentive schemes fail as often as they work if they are badly designed, as chapter five will show. So A. The cheap, dull practices pay most, which is exactly what the Mumbai experiment found, and exactly why it is puzzling that so many owners had not adopted them.
Experiment: Chapter four. The experiment, and why they had not done it.

The Island runs its own version of the experiment. Twenty-eight plants in seventeen firms; eleven firms, chosen at random, get the consultants. Randomizing by firm matters: plants in the same firm share an owner, and would share the practices. Here is weekly productivity, treated plants in green and the others in grey, measured against each plant's own past. The practices phase in over thirty weeks. Difference in differences over the following year: 21 percent higher, give or take 7, with the uncertainty computed firm by firm. Run the experiment many times on the Island and the estimates centre on the planted seventeen percent, scattering by about 3 points either way. That spread is the price of an experiment with seventeen firms, and it is why the real study's result, seventeen percent in the first year, was a surprise worth replicating.

So why had the owners not done it? The study's main answer is information: many owners had not heard of the practices, or did not believe they would help their own plant, until they saw them work. Time is the second: the owners ran everything themselves and would not delegate beyond the family, so their firms could not grow beyond what one person could watch. And nothing forced them: in protected, fragmented markets, badly run firms survive, chapter one's weak competition again. The result has travelled. In Mexico, Miriam Bruhn, Dean Karlan and Antoinette Schoar gave a year of consulting to small firms chosen at random among four hundred and thirty-two; productivity rose, and five years later the treated firms employed about half as many people again.
Personnel: Part fourteen built incentive theory. Personnel economics takes it into the firm, and its most famous case is a windscreen company. On the Island, a plant pays its installers by the hour, and they install the standard number of windscreens and no more, since effort above it is not paid. Switch to a piece rate, with the old wage guaranteed so nobody loses. The same people produce 20 percent more: the able ones now find extra effort worth it. And over time the workforce changes. The piece rate attracts people who are good at the job and keeps them, so output per worker rises 39 percent in all, about half of it from who joins rather than how hard anyone works. Edward Lazear found this at Safelite Glass when it switched its installers to piece rates in the 1990s: output per worker rose forty-four percent, with both effects at work, and about half of each worker's gain was passed on in higher pay. The catch is that piece rates pay for what is counted: output becomes more unequal, and quality, which is harder to count, needs watching.

Promotion is the second tool, and it has a famous flaw. Each of the Island's sales teams has eight people with two skills: selling, and managing other sellers. The two are only weakly related. Promote the best seller, and the new manager is a superb salesperson and an ordinary manager. Promote the best manager, if the firm could see who that is, and the team does far better: team sales rise about ten percent, against nothing for the best seller. Firms promote the best seller anyway, partly because selling is what they can see, and partly because the promotion is itself a prize that keeps the whole sales force working. The cost lands on the teams.

Called it? In 1969 Laurence Peter and Raymond Hull put it in a sentence: in a hierarchy every employee tends to rise to his level of incompetence. People are promoted for doing their present job well, until they reach one they do badly, and there they stay. Fifty years later Alan Benson, Danielle Li and Kelly Shue tested it with sales workers at a hundred and thirty-one firms. Firms do promote their best salespeople, and those salespeople make worse managers than colleagues who sold less. But firms limit the damage: where the manager's job carries more responsibility, they give sales less weight. The verdict: partly right. The principle holds where firms let it, and the cure is to promote on the skills of the next job, not the last.
CEOPay: Why are chief executives paid so much? One answer is a market. Xavier Gabaix and Augustin Landier assign managers to firms like Part seventeen's matching: the most talented to the largest firm. Talent differs only a little between the best chief executives and the five-hundredth, but a little more talent applied to a huge firm is worth a great deal, so firms bid for it. In equilibrium, across firms, pay rises with the firm's size to the power of about a third. The largest firm's chief executive earns 6.3 times as much as the two-hundred-and-fiftieth's. And if every firm grows six-fold, every chief executive's pay grows six-fold too, because what a manager is worth moves with the size of the firms bidding. That is what happened in America: chief executives' pay rose about six-fold between 1980 and 2003, and so did the market value of large companies. The theory explains the level without anyone behaving badly; it does not say the pay is deserved, only that it is what this market produces.

The other answer is that pay is set by people the chief executive has some influence over. A firm's results are partly the chief executive's skill and partly luck that everyone can see, such as the price of oil for an oil company. Part fourteen's theory says to pay for the first and filter out the second. On the Island, compare how pay responds to results, and to luck alone. A strong board pays for skill and nothing for luck. A weak board pays for luck as much as for skill. Marianne Bertrand and Sendhil Mullainathan found exactly this in American firms: pay rose with oil prices and exchange rates no chief executive set, and least where a large shareholder sat on the board to object. Their title said it: are chief executives rewarded for luck? The ones without principals are. How strongly a chief executive's own wealth moves with the shareholders' is one of this part's Dials.
Capital: How much should a firm borrow? Part twenty-three's Modigliani and Miller theorem is the starting point: with no taxes and no cost of going bust, the mix of debt and equity changes how the firm's value is divided, not its size. Add taxes: interest is deducted from taxable profit, so each dollar of debt saves twenty-one cents of tax at today's American rate. Add distress: the more a firm borrows, the likelier a bad year pushes it into default, where value is destroyed, by lost customers, forced sales and lawyers. Balancing the two, the Island's firm is worth most at about 55 percent debt, 9.8 percent more than with none. That is the trade-off theory, and its embarrassment is that real firms borrow less than it suggests, and the most profitable firms, which could carry the most debt, borrow least of all.

A second theory explains the embarrassment. Firms finance investment first from their own profits, then by borrowing, and issue new shares last. Stewart Myers and Nicholas Majluf's reason is Part thirteen's adverse selection: managers know more than investors, so a firm that sells shares signals that it thinks they are overpriced, and the price falls. Profitable firms have their own cash and never need to climb the ladder. And what do the people who decide say? John Graham and Campbell Harvey surveyed three hundred and ninety-two chief financial officers: for debt, financial flexibility and a good credit rating mattered most, more than the tax shield. Large firms used net present value and the capital asset pricing model, as the textbooks say; small firms often used the payback period, how long until the money comes back.
Governance: Michael Jensen and William Meckling's question in 1976: what happens when a firm's owner sells part of it and stays on as manager? The manager keeps a share alpha of the firm's value and enjoys perks: a jet, a grand office, a quiet life. Every dollar of perks costs the firm a dollar, but costs the manager only alpha dollars, so the manager takes perks until their value at the margin falls to alpha. Perks in red, the firm's value in blue. Owning it all, the manager takes 2; owning ten percent, 29. The loss is the agency cost of separating ownership from control, and outside investors, knowing it, pay less for the shares. Corporate governance is the list of remedies: boards that can fire the manager, large shareholders who watch, the threat of a takeover, debt that must be paid, and pay tied to the share price.

Who watches the manager in practice? Boards, though their members are often chosen with the chief executive's help; they are stronger when independent, and when a large owner sits among them, as chapter six's pay for luck showed. Activist investors, who buy a stake in order to push for change. And families, whose firms are most of the world's firms. Morten Bennedsen and colleagues studied Danish chief executive successions: when a family member took over, operating profitability fell by at least four percentage points. The trick behind that number is an instrument. Families that choose a successor are not random, so the authors used whether the departing chief executive's first child was a son, which makes a family successor likelier but has nothing else to do with the firm. Part four's tool, in the boardroom.
Buyouts: Private equity funds buy whole firms, usually with a great deal of borrowed money, and sell them some years later. Jensen saw them as the cure for chapter eight's agency problem: concentrated owners, managers who own a large stake, and debt that must be paid. Critics see job cuts. On the Island, three hundred buyouts are compared with twelve hundred similar firms. At the establishments the firms already had, jobs fall relative to the controls: -2.3 percent after two years, -5.1 after five. But the bought firms also open new establishments, and counting them, jobs at the whole firm do not fall. Productivity rises, mostly because weak plants close and better ones open. The Island was planted to echo the largest study, by Steven Davis and colleagues, using American census data: employment at target establishments fell three percent relative to controls within two years and six percent within five, while the targets created more jobs at new establishments and moved activity faster from weak plants to strong ones.

So what should one make of private equity? The case for: owners who watch, managers with a large stake, debt that disciplines, chapter eight's remedies in one package. The case against: debt that leaves no room for a bad year, large fees, and gains that may come from workers and suppliers rather than from efficiency. And the averages hide variety: results differ by era and by the kind of firm bought, with private firms bought out often growing and public firms taken private often shrinking. The habit that matters: compare with matched firms, follow the jobs to wherever they moved, and never stop at the first number.
WFH: Chapter eleven. Working from home, randomized.

Working from home is a question about organization that became a question for everyone in 2020. The Island runs the trial properly. 250 call-centre workers who volunteer to work from home; half, chosen at random, are sent home for forty weeks. At home they work more minutes a shift, with fewer breaks and sick days, and take more calls a minute, in a quieter room. In all, 15 percent more calls. And they quit far less often. These numbers were planted to echo a real trial.

The real trial came first. Nicholas Bloom, James Liang, John Roberts and Zhichun Jenny Ying randomized volunteers at Ctrip's call centre in Shanghai to work from home for nine months. Performance rose thirteen percent: nine points from working more minutes, four from more calls a minute. Quits fell sharply. But for the same performance, home workers were promoted less often. A decade later, a second trial at the same firm, now Trip.com, sent sixteen hundred graduate employees in engineering, marketing and finance home two days a week. Quits fell by a third, and performance reviews and promotions did not change. One caution: both studies had the firm's co-founder, James Liang, as an author, though the randomization is what makes them credible. And the effects depend on the job: measurable, independent tasks gain from quiet; the young, who learn by watching others, may lose.
Mergers: Chapter thirteen. Mergers that destroy value.

Firms also grow by buying other firms, and the record is sobering. Compare a diversified firm's value with the sum of its parts, each valued like a firm that does only that business. On the Island, diversified firms are worth 12.6 percent less. But the Island knows something an analyst would not: 5.9 points of that were there before the firms diversified, and only 6.7 came after. Philip Berger and Eli Ofek measured the discount in American firms from 1986 to 1991: thirteen to fifteen percent. Later work argued that much of it was selection: firms that chose to diversify were already worth less. The habit of chapter nine again: ask what the comparison would have shown before the event.

And the acquirers? Sara Moeller, Frederik Schlingemann and René Stulz added up what acquiring firms' shareholders lost around merger announcements from 1998 to 2001: two hundred and forty billion dollars, twelve cents for every dollar spent, against seven billion in the whole of the 1980s, most of it in a few deals by highly valued firms. The most famous of that wave was billed as a merger of equals: Daimler-Benz and Chrysler, in 1998, a deal of about thirty-six billion dollars. In 2007 Daimler sold eighty point one percent of Chrysler to the private equity firm Cerberus for seven point four billion. Why do acquirers overpay? Overconfident bidders, chief executives building empires, Part sixteen's winner's curse, and cultures, chapter twelve's relational contracts, that do not merge as easily as balance sheets.
Dials: Chapter fourteen. The Dials: management and CEO pay.

This part opens two Dials. The first: how much basic management practices add to productivity. The Mumbai experiment: 0.17, a sixth, within a year. The Island's version, planted to match, with the spread its seventeen firms allow. The status is settled within a range, because the one large randomized test is backed by smaller trials elsewhere that find gains of the same sign, measured in other ways. The practices are cheap, which leaves the puzzle of chapter four: why firms had not adopted them.

The second: when shareholders gain a thousand dollars, how much does the chief executive gain? Michael Jensen and Kevin Murphy, for 1974 to 1986: 3.25 dollars, counting pay, options, shares and the risk of being fired. They concluded that chief executives were paid like bureaucrats. Brian Hall and Jeffrey Liebman, for 1994, counting the whole portfolio of stock and options: 25.11 dollars for the average chief executive, and 5.29 for the median one. The status is contested: the answer depends on the years, on what is counted, and on whether the average or the typical executive is the question. Since the 1990s, holdings of stock and options, not salary, carry most of the incentive.
